passage: Tejas, you're scared of Bruno next door? Let me tell you about your Vinita Nani at your age. In our town, the milkman's boy got bitten by a street dog, and the whole lane talked about it for a week: the blood, the injections, the crying. After that I decided every dog in the world wanted to bite me. I crossed the road for puppies. I screamed at our neighbour's old dog, who could barely stand. Once my father asked, "How many dogs have bitten anyone you know?" I said, "Lots!" He made me count. It was one. One boy, one dog. But that one story was so loud in my head, it felt like hundreds.

qa.q: What happened to the milkman's boy?
qa.a: The milkman's boy got bitten by a street dog.

qa.q: Why did young Vinita feel every dog wanted to bite her?
qa.a: Young Vinita felt afraid because the bite story was retold for a week with vivid details, so it filled her mind and felt like something that happened all the time, even though it was one case.

qa.q: What did Vinita's father do that helped, and how could Tejas try it?
qa.a: He asked her to count real bites among people she knew, which showed there was only one. Tejas could count the gentle dogs seen on the street against any that actually bit someone.

qa.q: How might the owner of the neighbour's old dog have felt when young Vinita screamed?
qa.a: The owner may have felt puzzled or hurt, since their old dog could barely stand and had done nothing to frighten anyone.

grounding: Shows a child who, after one vivid dog-bite story, decides all dogs are dangerous because the memorable case feels common.

passage: The school van broke down, so Disha and her brother Anand had to walk the last kilometre home in the drizzle. At the corner by the tea stall, three street dogs lay curled under a cart. Disha froze. Two days earlier, a classmate had told everyone about a cousin bitten on the leg who needed a big injection. "They'll bite us," she whispered. "All dogs bite." Anand pointed. "Those three have slept there all year. You pass them every day in the van." "That's different," she said, gripping his sleeve. The rain got heavier. She made them walk the long way round, past the temple, adding ten wet minutes, and glared at every dog she saw.

qa.q: Why did Disha and Anand have to walk the last kilometre?
qa.a: The school van broke down, so they had to walk the last kilometre home in the drizzle.

qa.q: Why does Disha feel sure that all dogs bite?
qa.a: Disha feels frightened because the classmate's story of the bitten cousin and the big injection is fresh and scary. That fear feels more real than the many days the same dogs slept quietly by the cart.

qa.q: What small step could help Disha the next time they pass those dogs?
qa.a: Anand could help her count how many times she has passed them without trouble, and they could walk by calmly together, giving the dogs plenty of space.

qa.q: What is it like for Anand when Disha insists on the long way?
qa.a: Anand has to walk ten extra minutes in heavy rain, and may feel both annoyed and protective, since his calm facts can't beat her scary story.

grounding: Shows a girl who heard one vivid bite story deciding all dogs bite, even the ones she passes safely every day.

passage: Ever since the residents' group shared a clip of a boy being chased by a dog in another city, ten-year-old Zainab had refused to go down to the play area of their Tolichowki apartment block. "Moti will bite me," she said, though Moti, the watchman's brown dog, usually just slept by the gate and let the toddlers pull his ears. Rehana, her mother, sat with her on the balcony. "How many children here has Moti bitten?" Zainab thought. "None... but he could." "And how many times have you watched that clip?" "Eleven," Zainab admitted. "Everyone keeps sending it." Down below, her friends shrieked with laughter on the swings.

qa.q: How many times had Zainab watched the clip?
qa.a: Zainab admitted she had watched the clip eleven times.

qa.q: Why does Moti seem dangerous to Zainab even though he has bitten no one?
qa.a: Zainab is scared because the clip, sent again and again, fills her mind and makes a bite feel likely, even though Moti only sleeps and lets toddlers pull his ears.

qa.q: How could Rehana help Zainab get back to the play area?
qa.a: Rehana could go down with her, watch Moti together from a distance and notice how he actually behaves, while skipping new forwards of the clip for a while.

qa.q: How might Zainab's friends on the swings see her staying upstairs?
qa.a: They may miss her and not understand why, since to them Moti is just the sleepy dog by the gate.

grounding: Shows a girl who keeps seeing one scary dog clip deciding the gentle colony dog is dangerous.

passage:
"Zainab, come see! Pepper learned to sit!"
"No, Aditi baji. I'm staying on the sofa."
"She's a puppy. She's this big."
"Rehan in my class said a dog bit his neighbour's leg and he needed injections. Dogs bite."
Aditi's mother came in with a plate of pakoras. "Zainab, how many dogs do you know?"
Zainab thought. "Pepper. Nanu's dog. The shop dog. The white one at school."
"Have any of them bitten anyone?"
"...No. But Rehan's story."
"One story is very loud, isn't it?" said Aditi's mother. "It shouts over all the quiet ones."
Pepper wobbled over and sniffed Zainab's sock. Zainab pulled her feet up fast. Then, very slowly, she put one finger down. Pepper licked it.
"Eww," said Zainab. But she didn't pull back.

qa.q: What trick had Pepper learned?
qa.a: Pepper learned to sit.

qa.q: Why does it feel true to Zainab that dogs bite?
qa.a: Rehan's bite story made Zainab scared, and because it was so easy to remember it seemed like what dogs usually do. The many dogs she knows that never bit anyone didn't come to mind.

qa.q: What choice did Zainab make at the end, and why was it a good small step?
qa.a: She slowly put one finger down for Pepper. Testing the fear a little at a time let a real, gentle dog start to outweigh the scary story.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel when Zainab refuses to meet Pepper?
qa.a: Aditi is probably disappointed, since she was excited to show off the new puppy, and may want her cousin to see how gentle Pepper is.

grounding: A young girl hears one scary dog-bite story and decides all dogs bite, even a small puppy at her cousin's home.

passage: I'm Vaibhav, and as a boy of nine I feared every dog in the world. It started when my cousin Indu told me about a boy at her school who got bitten by a stray. She did the growl and the scream. After that, I saw that bite whenever I saw a dog. I crossed the road when I saw Bholu, our neighbour's old dog, though he just sleeps by the gate and had licked my hand a hundred times. I told Ma, "All dogs bite, it's true, Indu said." Ma asked, "How many dogs have bitten you?" None. I still didn't pat Bholu for a long time. Now I do. He's very soft. And Indu admits she made the growl louder than it was.

qa.q: What was the name of the neighbour's old dog?
qa.a: Bholu.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav cross the road even to avoid Bholu?
qa.a: Indu's dramatic story with the growl and the scream was so vivid that it came to mind every time he saw any dog. It felt more real than all the times Bholu had licked his hand.

qa.q: What question from Ma could help Vaibhav, and how might he use it next time?
qa.a: "How many dogs have bitten you?" Next time a scary story makes him afraid, he can count what has really happened to him before deciding something is always true.

qa.q: How might Indu feel knowing her story scared Vaibhav for so long?
qa.a: She might feel a bit guilty, which is why she now admits she made the growl louder than it was.

grounding: A boy recalls how one vivid bite story from his cousin made him fear every dog, even a gentle old neighbour's dog.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today at lunch Dilnaz told us her cousin in Bhopal got bitten by a street dog and had to go to the hospital again and again. She said the dog came out of nowhere, growling, with its teeth showing. I could not eat my paratha after that.
On the way home, Bruno from the second floor wagged at me like always. I ran up the stairs so fast I dropped my water bottle. Mummy asked why. I said ALL dogs bite, Dilnaz said so. Mummy said Bruno has lived here six years and never bitten anyone. I said he just hasn't YET.
I am never going near any dog again. Not even Bruno.
Sarita

qa.q: What did Sarita drop while running up the stairs?
qa.a: Sarita dropped the water bottle.

qa.q: Why is Sarita so sure all dogs bite?
qa.a: Sarita feels scared, because Dilnaz's story was so vivid that one bite now seems like what every dog does, even Bruno.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Sarita feel safer around Bruno?
qa.a: She could stand with Sarita and watch Bruno from a little distance, talk about the gentle dogs they know, and show calm ways to be near a dog.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz had told a story about a friendly dog instead?
qa.a: Sarita would probably remember that story most and greet Bruno as usual; the vivid story, not what dogs usually do, is steering the fear.

grounding: A child's diary shows one vivid dog-bite story turning into a belief that all dogs bite, even a familiar gentle one.

passage: The path to the gurdwara school ran past the Sandhus' farm, where old Moti lay in the shade every morning. For two years Baljeet had walked past him. Then on Sunday, at the tubewell, cousin Preeti told everyone how a dog in the next village had bitten a boy on the leg, how he screamed, how there was blood on his kurta. That night Baljeet dreamt of teeth. On Monday he stopped dead at the farm gate. "I'm going the long way," he said, and walked twenty minutes round the sugarcane, arriving late with muddy chappals. When his Bebe asked why, he said, "Dogs bite. Preeti said." "Which dogs?" "All of them." Moti, meanwhile, had not even lifted his head.

qa.q: Where did Moti lie every morning?
qa.a: In the shade at the Sandhus' farm.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet choose the long way round?
qa.a: He felt frightened because Preeti's story of the bitten boy was so vivid that it seemed any dog, even old Moti, might bite.

qa.q: What small step could help Baljeet?
qa.a: An adult could walk the old path with him, point out that Moti has lain there calmly for two years, and show him how to pass dogs calmly.

qa.q: What would change if Preeti had also talked about the many village dogs that never bite?
qa.a: Baljeet might see the bite as rare rather than normal, and keep walking his usual path past Moti.

grounding: After one vivid bite story, a boy decides all dogs bite and avoids a calm farm dog he has passed for two years.

passage: Clara's birthday invitation had a puppy on it, because Clara had a real one now, a fluffy beagle called Pip. Sofia put the card face down on her desk in their Madrid flat. At dinner on Sunday her uncle had told the story of a neighbour's dog that bit a delivery man, with a hand wrapped in bandages and a trip to hospital. Sofia had heard it once, but she kept seeing the bandages. "I can't go," she told her mother. "Clara's dog will bite." "Pip is ten weeks old," said her mother. "He mostly sleeps." "That's what everyone thinks. Then they bite." Her mother sat down beside her. "How many dogs do you know, Sofia?" Sofia counted: Pip, the baker's dog, Grandma's old Luna. None of them had ever bitten anyone.

qa.a: Pip, a fluffy beagle.

qa.q: Why does Sofia feel sure Pip will bite?
qa.a: She feels scared because her uncle's bite story, with its bandages, keeps playing in her mind, so one case feels like what all dogs do.

qa.q: Why is her mother's question a good step?
qa.a: Counting the dogs Sofia really knows shows that none of them has bitten anyone, which balances the single scary story.

qa.q: How might Clara feel if Sofia skipped the party because of Pip?
qa.a: Clara would likely be disappointed and confused that her friend stayed away because of a sleepy puppy.

passage: At the primary school in Mysuru, a brown dog slept every afternoon under the neem tree by the gate. On Monday, Tushar's classmate told the class a long story about his cousin's dog bite: blood, a hospital, injections in the stomach. Tushar listened with wide eyes. On Tuesday, he refused to walk past the neem tree. He waited inside the gate until Rekha ma'am came. "All dogs bite," he said. "They're all dangerous." Rekha ma'am said, "Tushar, this dog has slept here for two years. Has it ever bitten anyone?" Tushar thought. No. He had even patted it once. But the cousin's story felt bigger. "It could," he said, and stamped his foot, angry that she didn't believe him. Rekha ma'am walked him past the tree, holding his hand. The dog didn't even open its eyes.

qa.q: Where did the brown dog sleep every afternoon?
qa.a: Under the neem tree by the gate.

qa.q: Why did Tushar feel so sure all dogs are dangerous?
qa.a: The vivid bite story felt huge and scary, so it seemed like what dogs usually do, and he felt afraid and angry that Rekha ma'am doubted him.

qa.q: How could Rekha ma'am help Tushar see the dog more fairly?
qa.a: She could remind him how many days he's walked past safely, and let him watch the dog calmly from a distance each day.

qa.q: How might Rekha ma'am feel when Tushar stamps his foot?
qa.a: Rekha ma'am likely feels patient and understanding, knowing the fear came from the story.

grounding: It shows a child who decides all dogs are dangerous after one vivid bite story, treating the most memorable case as the most common.

passage:
Sunday. At a cousin's birthday in Kolkata, an uncle told a loud story about a street dog biting a boy on the leg. Abhinav, seven, sat very still.

Wednesday. On the walk to school, Abhinav clutched his sister Lavanya's hand and pulled her across the road whenever he saw a dog, even old Bhola from their lane. "All dogs bite. Uncle said." When she tried to let go, he got angry and shouted.

Saturday. Lavanya counted with him. "How many dogs did we pass this week?" They counted on fingers. Twenty-two. "How many bit anyone?" Abhinav was quiet. "None." "And how many stories did you hear?" "One." He looked at Bhola, lying in the sun. He still held her hand tight, but he didn't pull her across the road.

qa.q: How many dogs did Abhinav and Lavanya count that week?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav feel sure that all dogs bite?
qa.a: The uncle's vivid story stuck, so it felt like the usual thing, making him scared and angry when Lavanya tried to let go.

qa.q: What did Lavanya's counting help Abhinav see?
qa.a: It showed that twenty-two dogs passed without biting and only one story existed, helping him compare the vivid case to real life.

qa.q: How might Bhola seem to Lavanya compared with how Abhinav saw him?
qa.a: To Lavanya, Bhola is just the harmless old dog from their lane, lying in the sun; to Abhinav, after the story, he seemed like a danger.

grounding: It shows a child who decides all dogs are dangerous after one vivid story, until counting real encounters helps, over several days.

passage: Pranav, scared of the neighbour's dog after your friend's story? When I was a boy of eight, in Shillong, the tea-shop man told a story about a mad dog biting a boy, with snarling and running and crying. After that, I was sure every dog in the world wanted to bite me. Even our neighbour's old dog, Kalu, who slept on our doorstep. I shouted at my mother when she asked me to buy bread. One day she sat with me and said, "Anirban, how many times has Kalu bitten you?" "Never." "How many dogs have bitten anyone you know?" "Only the one in the story." She let me sit with Kalu, just touching his ear. Slowly, I remembered he was my friend.

qa.q: What was the name of the neighbour's old dog?
qa.a: Kalu.

qa.q: Why did young Anirban feel every dog wanted to bite him?
qa.a: The vivid tea-shop story felt so real that it seemed common, making him scared and angry enough to shout at his mother.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Anirban?
qa.a: His mother asked how often Kalu or any dog had actually bitten anyone, and then let him touch Kalu's ear, helping real experience outweigh the story.

qa.q: How might Anirban's mother have felt when he shouted about the bread?
qa.a: She probably felt worried and patient, realising the story had frightened him.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, one vivid dog-bite story made all dogs seem dangerous.

passage:
It was Holi, and Jaya had to take the gujiyas to Charu's house before the colours started. The quickest way was down the lane with the brown dog.

Last night, her cousin had told a story about a boy whose leg was bitten so badly he needed twenty stitches. Jaya had dreamed about it.

Now she stood at the corner with the plate. The brown dog lay in the sun, tail thumping. Jaya's heart hammered. All dogs bite. That's what dogs do.

The long way would take twenty minutes.

Charu's grandmother saw her from the balcony. "Jaya! Moti won't hurt you. He's been here ten years and never bitten anyone."

Jaya didn't move. Ten years felt smaller than twenty stitches.

qa.a: He needed twenty stitches.

qa.q: Why did Jaya feel sure all dogs bite?
qa.a: Jaya felt scared because the vivid story of twenty stitches filled her mind, so one bad case felt like what all dogs do.

qa.q: What could Charu's grandmother try next to help Jaya?
qa.a: She could come down and walk Jaya past Moti, showing calmly how gentle he is, one small step at a time.

qa.q: How might Charu's grandmother see Jaya's fear?
qa.a: Charu's grandmother probably finds it a bit puzzling, since Moti has been gentle for ten years, but likely wants to help Jaya feel safe.

"So?"

passage:
Last Diwali, my cousin told us a story about a dog in his colony that bit a boy on the leg. He showed us the scar on the boy's photo. I'm Pankaj, and I was nine, and I couldn't stop thinking about it.
After that, every dog looked dangerous. The old brown dog that sleeps outside our building, who never even barks, suddenly seemed like a wolf. I crossed the road whenever I saw him. When my friend Dilnaz stroked him, I shouted at her to stop.
"He's been here since we were babies," she said. "He's never bitten anyone."
I didn't believe her. One story felt bigger than all those years.
It took till the winter holidays, when Dilnaz and I counted every dog we passed for a week, forty-one dogs and zero bites, before the fear started to shrink.

qa.q: How many dogs did Pankaj and Dilnaz count in a week?
qa.a: They counted forty-one dogs and zero bites.

qa.q: Why did the old brown dog suddenly seem dangerous to Pankaj?
qa.a: The vivid bite story left Pankaj frightened, so one memorable case felt like proof that every dog was dangerous.

qa.q: What helped the fear start to shrink, and why?
qa.a: Counting real dogs for a week with Dilnaz gave Pankaj actual numbers, forty-one dogs and no bites, which showed that bites are rare.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when Pankaj shouted at her to stop stroking the dog?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and a little annoyed, since the dog had been gentle for years.
